newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Expansionary Irish budget seen, inflation worries.
newsitem.headline: Expansionary Irish budget seen, inflation worries.

text.p: Finance minister Ruairi Quinn will please Irish voters with an expansionary pre-election budget on Wednesday but worry a central bank already concerned about an overly strong currency as it prepares for EMU.
"The budget will undoubtedly be expansionary. I do not know if it will be too loose for the central bank to digest but they certainly won't like it," one leading economist said.

Other countries are hamstrung by soaring budget deficits but Ireland's public finances are in the best shape for 20 years, giving a coalition government with waning popularity a chance to give back some of the spoils before an election due by November.
Economists expect the government to spend up to 400 million punts ($650 million) cutting taxes. Ireland, one of the strongest growing EU economies, can afford it.
The exchequer borrowing requirement (EBR) for 1996 was 437 million punts, 1.2 percent of GNP, compared with the official budget day target for 1996 of 729 million or 2.0 percent of GNP.
The 1996 current budget was in surplus to the tune of 292 million as against an expected deficit of 82 million punts.

"I am forecasting a post-budget EBR of 585 million punts or 1.5 percent of GNP, comprising a current budget surplus of 240 million and capital borrowing of 825 million," Bloxham stockbroker's economist Alan McQuaid told Reuters.
NCB stockbrokers chief economist Dermot O'Brien sees the finance minister giving himself more room for manoeuvre in 1997.
"We estimate a post-budget EBR of 755 million," O'Brien said. Riada's Padhraic Garvey is expecting 700 million.
Even after a give-away budget all post-budget borrowing estimates leave Ireland comfortably below Maastricht's guideline 3.0 percent borrowing target.
All economists agree that Quinn will unveil some very generous tax cuts on the day but remain at odds as to what the Central Bank's response will be to the goverment's generousity.
Further stimuli to inflation, which may increase pressure to tighten monetary policy, is not the Central Bank's favoured outcome as the Irish pound hugs the ceiling of the ERM grid.
McQuaid expects the Central Bank to raise rates by a quarter point by the end of the first quarter as a shot across the bows against any inflation-stimulating spending spree by consumers.

Riada's Garvey said the Bank is more likely to contain its action to tightening interbank money market rates, while NCB's O'Brien said the Central Bank has too many other worries to risk an interest rate moves at this time.
The Irish pound has gained more than 10 percent on the German mark over the last six months and is at the top of the Exchange Rate Mechanism.

Economists are expecting a rising inflationary trend which may average out at 2.5 percent for the year. They expect this may still satisfy Maastricht in 1997 but is likely to run into trouble in 1998 unless the economy begins to slow down.

Maastricht guidelines states that inflation must not exceed that of the three best-performing EU states by more than 1.5 percent but it also requires members to maintain a stable and credible exchange rate. ($1=.6110 Punt)
